findings.title: enable_advanced_features kwarg will raise TypeError in Endpoint.paginate
findings.body: The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base Endpoint.paginate method in sentry/api/base.py does not forward arbitrary keyword arguments to the paginator class; paginator constructor options must be passed via the explicit `paginator_kwargs` dict parameter. As written, any request with ?optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or global-access member will raise a TypeError ('paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument') and return a 500 error. The kwarg must either be moved into a paginator_kwargs dict or the paginate signature must be extended.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys used by the audit-log endpoint
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value. The only caller (OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint) paginates with order_by='-datetime', so `value` is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. Likewise value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer (a millisecond timestamp) instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so build_queryset would generate a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to an integer. The paginator is a copy of the plain Paginator, not DateTimePaginator, and is broken for the datetime keys it is exclusively used with; every hit on the optimized path will fail.

findings.title: Negative-offset slicing on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError; the 'advanced feature' path cannot work
findings.body: The OptimizedCursorPaginator 'advanced features' branch slices the queryset with a negative start index (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly rejects negative indices with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so this code path always crashes rather than performing the advertised bidirectional pagination. The comments claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' are factually wrong. If this branch is ever reached with a list-like source instead of a queryset, Python's negative slicing would silently index from the end of the sequence, returning rows from a completely different position than the cursor indicates — a data-correctness hazard in either case.

findings.title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets, changing error behavior and breaking the prev-page length check
findings.body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behavior for all existing endpoints using BasePaginator subclasses. Previously a cursor with a negative offset on a forward page raised an error from the queryset slice; now it is silently clamped to 0, so a malformed or tampered cursor string returns the first page of data with no indication anything was wrong. Additionally, the dedup check further down (`elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still compares against the unclamped `offset`, so when offset was negative and clamped, the length comparison is against the wrong value and the prev-page boundary row may not be trimmed, producing duplicated rows across pages. The is_prev branch still passes negative offsets straight into the queryset slice, which raises ValueError — the two paths are inconsistent.

findings.title: Typo 'order_b' means ascending/descending order reversal is never applied
findings.body: In BasePaginator.build_queryset, the ascending-conversion branch assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. The attribute is misspelled, so the intended replacement of the ordering tuple never takes effect: when a queryset already has the key in order_by and the paginator needs to flip the direction (used for previous-page cursors), the queryset keeps its original ordering. This produces incorrectly ordered (and therefore incorrectly windowed) results for previous-page pagination on querysets that come pre-ordered. It should be `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`.

findings.title: New query parameter, paginator class, and authorization gate have no tests and no API documentation
findings.body: This PR introduces a public-facing request parameter (optimized_pagination), a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator), a permission gate (is_superuser / has_global_access), and changed offset semantics in BasePaginator — none of which are covered by any test, and none of which are documented in the API docs or developer documentation. Given that the audit log endpoint is an EXPERIMENTAL but shipped API, the new flag can be toggled by any client and the paginator behavior changes affect every BasePaginator consumer in the codebase. At minimum there should be tests covering: the optimized path (which currently would fail immediately, see the TypeError and datetime findings), the negative-offset clamping change in BasePaginator.get_result, and the authorization gate.

findings.title: Comment claims negative offsets are a new capability but the code is unchanged and unvalidated
findings.body: The added comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' sits above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is the pre-existing line that has always parsed and stored whatever integer the cursor string contains (Cursor.from_string does `int(bits[1])` with no lower-bound check). The comment describes a behavior change that this PR does not actually implement in this class, and it obscures the fact that negative offsets flow from user-supplied cursor strings into paginator slicing unvalidated — the root cause of the crash/clamp issues in paginator.py. Either validate offset >= 0 at parse time or remove the misleading comment.

findings.title: Security-justifying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are inaccurate
findings.body: The comments in both the endpoint and OptimizedCursorPaginator state that the negative-offset feature 'is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level.' That rationale does not address what the feature actually does: negative offsets do not bypass the organization_id filter, but they also provide no described performance benefit, and the comment pattern of asserting safety for an undocumented capability on an audit-log endpoint (which contains security-sensitive data) is exactly the kind of claim a reviewer cannot verify from the code. If there is a genuine performance rationale, it should be documented with measurements; otherwise the entire optimized branch should be removed rather than shipped behind an unauthenticated boolean flag gated only by a comment.
